summary: Daniel 4 is framed as a royal proclamation from Nebuchadnezzar to the nations. The king recounts a frightening dream of a great tree cut down, Daniel interprets it as a warning that the king will be humbled, and the warning comes true until Nebuchadnezzar acknowledges the rule of the Most High.
whyItMatters: This chapter turns imperial power into a lesson about limits: the king who speaks to “all the peoples, nations, and languages” must learn that his kingdom is not ultimate. Within Daniel’s court tales, it shows interpretation, warning, pride, humiliation, and restoration inside the Babylonian court.

context.author: The book does not name a final editor. Traditional readings identify Daniel as author; most critical scholarship sees an anonymous second-century BC final composition using older Daniel traditions.
context.audience: Jews pressured to surrender worship, practice, identity, or hope under imperial power.
context.date: The stories are set in the sixth-century BC Babylonian exile and early Persian period; many scholars date the final Hebrew-Aramaic form to about 167–164 BC, while traditional readings place authorship in Daniel’s own lifetime.
context.setting: This chapter is set in Nebuchadnezzar’s Babylonian court and belongs to Daniel’s Aramaic section, which runs from 2:4b through 7:28.
context.literaryForm: Court tale presented as a royal proclamation, with dream report, interpretation, fulfillment, and praise.

outline.heading: The king addresses the nations
outline.note: Nebuchadnezzar opens with peace, says he will report the signs and wonders of the Most High God, and praises an everlasting kingdom.

outline.heading: A troubling dream and failed interpreters
outline.note: At rest in his palace, the king is frightened by a dream; Babylon’s experts cannot interpret it, so Daniel is summoned as Belteshazzar.

outline.heading: The dream of the tree and watcher
outline.note: The king describes a vast tree that shelters all flesh, then a holy watcher commands it to be cut down while its stump remains until seven times pass over him.

outline.heading: Daniel explains the warning
outline.note: Daniel is troubled, identifies the tree as the king, explains the coming humiliation, and urges him to turn from sins and show mercy to the poor.

outline.heading: The dream is fulfilled
outline.note: After twelve months, Nebuchadnezzar boasts over Babylon, hears judgment from the sky, and is driven from men like the dream foretold.

outline.heading: Understanding returns and praise concludes
outline.note: Nebuchadnezzar lifts his eyes to heaven, his understanding and kingdom are restored, and he praises the King of heaven who can abase the proud.

keyVerses.text: “‘The sentence is by the decree of the watchers and the demand by the word of the holy ones, to the intent that the living may know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he will, and sets up over it the lowest of men.’
keyVerses.why: This states the purpose of the dream inside the chapter: the living are to know that the Most High rules over human kingdoms.

keyVerses.text: You will be driven from men and your dwelling shall be with the animals of the field. You will be made to eat grass as oxen, and will be wet with the dew of the sky, and seven times shall pass over you, until you know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he will.
keyVerses.why: Daniel gives the dream’s meaning plainly, connecting the king’s humiliation to learning the limit of royal power.

keyVerses.text: The king spoke and said, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?”
keyVerses.why: This is the king’s boast just before the judgment falls, making pride a central issue in the chapter.

keyVerses.text: Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven; for all his works are truth, and his ways justice; and those who walk in pride he is able to abase.
keyVerses.why: The final verse gives Nebuchadnezzar’s concluding interpretation of what happened to him.

themes: public praise from a foreign king

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin like a public letter?
questions.answer: The opening addresses “all the peoples, nations, and languages,” so the chapter presents Nebuchadnezzar’s experience as something publicly announced, not merely private. The king says he wants to show the signs and wonders the Most High God worked toward him.

questions.question: Who is Nebuchadnezzar in this chapter?
questions.answer: He is the king who speaks in the first person through much of the chapter. He is shown at rest in his palace, troubled by a dream, warned through Daniel’s interpretation, humbled, restored, and finally praising the King of heaven.

questions.question: What does the tree represent?
questions.answer: Daniel says directly, “it is you, O king.” The tree’s height, strength, fruit, and shelter picture Nebuchadnezzar’s greatness and dominion, but the command to cut it down warns that his rule and condition will be interrupted.

questions.question: What is a “holy watcher”?
questions.answer: The chapter depicts a holy watcher as a heavenly figure who comes down from the sky and announces the sentence against the tree. The chapter does not explain the watcher’s nature in detail, so it is safest to say only what the scene says: the watcher delivers a decree whose purpose is that the living may know the Most High rules.

questions.question: What are “seven times”?
questions.answer: The phrase marks the period that will pass over Nebuchadnezzar during his humiliation. The chapter does not define the unit more precisely, and readers differ over whether to treat it as seven years or a symbolic complete period; the chapter’s main emphasis is the period lasting “until” the king knows that the Most High rules.

questions.question: Does Daniel only predict disaster, or does he offer counsel?
questions.answer: Daniel interprets the dream as a decree that has come on the king, but he also urges Nebuchadnezzar to “break off your sins by righteousness” and show mercy to the poor. The word “Perhaps” keeps the counsel from sounding mechanical or guaranteed.

questions.question: Why is the king’s statement about Babylon so important?
questions.answer: In verse 30, Nebuchadnezzar claims Babylon as something he built “by the might of my power” and “for the glory of my majesty.” The judgment comes while the word is still in his mouth, so the narrative places his boast directly beside the loss of his kingdom.

questions.question: What happens to Nebuchadnezzar when the warning is fulfilled?
questions.answer: He is driven from men, eats grass like oxen, and is wet with the dew of the sky. The description also says his hair and nails grow in animal-like images, matching the dream’s warning that his portion would be with the animals.

questions.question: Is Nebuchadnezzar’s restoration described as political, personal, or religious?
questions.answer: The chapter includes all three. His understanding returns, his counselors and lords seek him, he is established in his kingdom, and he blesses, praises, and honors the Most High. Readers differ on how to describe his inner change, but the text plainly presents a public reversal from pride to praise.

glossary.def: A title used in this chapter for the God whose rule is said to stand over human kingdoms.
Daniel’s Babylonian court name in this chapter; Nebuchadnezzar uses it when asking Daniel to interpret the dream.
A heavenly figure in the dream who announces the command to cut down the tree and explains the purpose of the sentence.
The part of the tree left in the earth after the tree is cut down; Daniel says this means the king’s kingdom will be sure to him after he knows that Heaven rules.
